source: Kemp & Tenenbaum (2009) Structured statistical models of inductive reasoning
finding: Property induction is posed as inference about a partly observed feature vector over known categories. A Bayesian learner has a prior over all possible extensions of a new property. The prior is built from structured background knowledge (tree, 2D space, causal graph, threshold). Different structures give different inductive contexts.
numbers: Four models (taxonomic, spatial, threshold, causal). Five datasets for the default biological context: Osherson-specific, Osherson-mammals, Smith fox, Smith elephant, Smith mammals.
quote: Everyday inductive inferences are often guided by rich background knowledge.
limits: Priors are hand-chosen structures plus fitted parameters; learning of structure is only sketched. Fits are to averaged human ratings of argument strength.
agent_relevance: Supports a design where the agent first names the relevant structure (taxonomy, causal links, threshold) and only then generalises. Similarity alone is the wrong default when the property is not blank.

source: Kemp & Tenenbaum (2009) Structured statistical models of inductive reasoning
finding: Taxonomic model (tree plus diffusion process plus Bayesian inference) fits the five default-context datasets very well. The tree, the diffusion prior and the Bayesian engine each matter: swapping the tree for a 2D space hurts mainly the diversity data; a memory-based prior cannot capture diversity.
numbers: Tree+diffusion r = .96, .90, .95, .96, .85 over the five datasets (row read from the figure text; column order inferred). 2D spatial model is poor on Osherson-mammals (r about .64) which needs diversity. Memory-based raw model r about .81 to .96 but fails on diversity.
limits: Correlations were extracted from figure text, so the column-to-dataset mapping is inferred. Fit to mean ratings, not to individual people.
agent_relevance: Diversity of evidence needs a model with structure; a flat nearest-neighbour rule cannot give it. For the agent: spread test cases across the space of hypotheses, do not pile them near one another.

source: Kemp & Tenenbaum (2009) Structured statistical models of inductive reasoning
finding: The same paper summarises the standard phenomena: similarity, typicality (seals->mammals weaker than horses->mammals), diversity (seals, squirrels->mammals stronger than horses, rhinos->mammals). Osherson et al. identify 13 qualitative phenomena. Context changes the pattern: a bear disease is judged more likely in salmon than in moose (ecological reasoning), whereas anatomical properties follow taxonomy.
numbers: Osherson et al. (1990): 13 phenomena. Sloman (1993) adds more.
quote: given that a certain disease is found in bears, it may seem more likely that the disease is found in salmon than in moose
limits: Review statement; original numbers are in Osherson et al. 1990 which was not opened.
agent_relevance: Before generalising, the agent should label the inductive context (blank taxonomic property vs causal or ecological property). The same premises can point in opposite directions.

source: Kemp & Tenenbaum (2009) Structured statistical models of inductive reasoning
finding: Describes the similarity-coverage model as a linear combination of (1) similarity of conclusion to premises and (2) coverage of the smallest superordinate category containing premises and conclusion. Compared with Sloman's feature-based model and Heit's Bayesian proposal (prior from properties retrieved from memory, no formal way to generate the prior).
numbers: SCM has one free parameter in their fits; SCM with human similarity ratings does better than with feature covariance.
limits: Authors' own competitor description; they are partisans of the Bayesian structured view.
agent_relevance: SCM is a cheap, code-computable score. It can rank candidate generalisations, but only for blank properties.

source: Tenenbaum, Kemp & Shafto (2007) Theory-based Bayesian models of inductive reasoning
finding: Spells out why SCM is arbitrary: coverage is the average over category members of the MAXIMUM similarity to the premises (MaxSim). The alternative SumSim (summed similarity) fails on general arguments. The non-linearity is what lets a similarity model show diversity.
numbers: Five datasets (Osherson specific: 36 two-premise arguments with conclusion horses; Osherson general: 45 three-premise arguments with conclusion mammals; three Smith sets). Evolutionary (Bayesian tree) model r = .93, .92, .89, .98, .80. MaxSim r = .71, .79, .93, .94, .84. Raw-feature model r = .70, .27, .77, .95, .68. SumSim r = .74, -.34, .85, .92, -.02. Strict tree r = .56, .50, .56, .85, .67.
quote: the poor performance of SumSim calls into question the explanatory value of similarity-based approaches
limits: Models were run on feature-rating similarities, which lowers MaxSim relative to Osherson's own human similarity ratings. Row order read from figure text.
agent_relevance: A concrete result: summing evidence from similar cases is worse than taking best coverage. Diverse premises beat many near-duplicate premises. Useful for the agent's check on how many independent examples back a rule.

source: Tenenbaum, Kemp & Shafto (2007) Theory-based Bayesian models of inductive reasoning
finding: Explains why SumSim cannot give diversity: its total strength is linear in the single-premise strengths, so it prefers premises that are each strongest alone, and those are similar to each other (horses, cows, rhinos beat horses, seals, squirrels for the conclusion mammals). Strict-tree model gives 100% to every set that spans the same node, so it cannot show graded diversity.
numbers: See a05 for r values.
limits: Argument from the authors' own model comparison.
agent_relevance: Argues for graded, soft hypothesis weighting rather than hard category membership when judging evidence.

source: Hampton & Cannon (2004) Category-based induction: an effect of conclusion typicality (Memory & Cognition 32)
finding: Typicality of the CONCLUSION category (not only the premise) raises inductive strength. This is not predicted by SCM (which only uses premise typicality via coverage). Familiarity ruled out as a confound.
numbers: Exp 1 regression, 22 triplets (8 mammals, 7 birds, 7 insects), 36 raters of strength: per-participant regressions with 18 raters, mean R = .40, similarity beta = -.34 (t(17) = -8.00, p<.001), conclusion typicality beta = -.12 (t(17) = -3.27, p<.005), premise typicality ns. Exp 3 forced choice, N = 48: typical conclusion chosen 58% (chance 50), t(47) = 3.89, 34 of 48 participants, 17 of 22 items. Exp 2 (N = 18) familiarity r = .1 with the effect.
quote: people are more willing to project properties to more typical conclusions
limits: Small effect. Ratings from separate groups of students at one university. Example: vultures->robins preferred over vultures->ostriches.
agent_relevance: A known bias: a conclusion that looks typical feels better supported. The agent should not let how typical a target looks raise its confidence.

source: Hampton & Cannon (2004) Category-based induction: an effect of conclusion typicality
finding: The paper tests three alternative accounts of the typicality effect and discusses implications for Osherson et al. (1990) and Sloman (1993). One rival is that typical conclusions cue a narrower superordinate (duck+canary -> flying birds) so coverage is higher. The authors treat that as a defence open to SCM, so SCM is not cleanly refuted.
numbers: Not given; qualitative discussion.
limits: I read the discussion start only; the three alternatives were not all read in full.
agent_relevance: Shows that the choice of reference class (superordinate) changes the inductive judgment. The agent should state its reference class explicitly.

source: Tenenbaum (1999) A Bayesian framework for concept learning, PhD thesis MIT; Tenenbaum & Griffiths (2001) BBS 24
finding: Search-result abstract only: smaller consistent hypotheses are more likely than larger ones, and exponentially more so as examples accumulate (size principle). With hypothesis averaging, generalisation moves from similarity-like to rule-like as examples grow.
numbers: None read from the source.
limits: Not opened (the thesis download returned an HTML page and the BBS PDF host failed). Secondary description only.
agent_relevance: See a10 for the formula, read from a teaching page.

source: Gureckis lab course notes: Bayesian number game (demo of Tenenbaum 1999, 2001)
finding: Number game model: hypotheses are 34 maths rules (squares, cubes, primes, powers of 2 to 10, multiples 3 to 12, even, odd, ending in 0 to 9) plus 5,050 intervals in 1..100. Size-principle likelihood P(X|h) = (1/|h|)^n if all examples lie in h. Prediction is P(y in C | X) = sum over h of P(y in h) P(h|X).
numbers: Prior lambda = 2/3 on maths rules, 1-lambda on intervals. After the single example 16: powers of 4 .33, powers of 2 .16, squares .10, ending in 6 .10. After 16, 8, 2, 64: powers of 2 likelihood (1/6)^4 about .00077 vs even numbers (1/50)^4 = .00000016.
quote: Smaller hypotheses that are consistent with the data get higher likelihood
limits: Secondary teaching page, not the original paper; hypothesis space and prior are from a homework version, not the human experiment. Weak sampling (likelihood 1) is offered as a contrast.
agent_relevance: Directly codeable. The agent can enumerate candidate rules, score each by (1/|h|)^n, and average predictions instead of picking one rule. This is the 'suspicious coincidence' check.

source: Gigerenzer & Hoffrage (1995) How to improve Bayesian reasoning without instruction: frequency formats (Psych Review 102)
finding: Same problem, different format: natural frequencies make Bayesian reasoning far more common than probabilities. Verbal write-aloud protocols were coded for the algorithm used.
numbers: Study 1: 60 Salzburg students, 15 problems each in two of four versions (format x menu), 30 tasks per person, 1,774 solutions coded. Share of Bayesian algorithms: probability format 16% (standard menu) and 28% (short menu); frequency format 46% (standard) and 50% (short). Format effect about 29.9 and 21.6 points; menu effect 12.1 and 3.7 points. Mammography: 43.3% of participants gave a frequency answer of 8 out of 103 (7.8%).
quote: Probability formats, in contrast, elicited 16% and 28%
limits: Even in the best condition only about half of answers were Bayesian. Students, paid, wrote aloud for about an hour. Some problems were not medical.
agent_relevance: Strong support for a code step that converts any probability problem to counts out of a fixed number (for example 1,000) before reasoning. Cheap and reliable.

source: Gigerenzer & Hoffrage (1995) How to improve Bayesian reasoning without instruction: frequency formats
finding: Study 2 shows that relative frequencies (percent) do NOT help: the benefit comes from natural (absolute) frequencies, which carry the base rate. The short menu (joint counts) makes the Bayesian calculation a simple ratio. Common non-Bayesian algorithms: joint occurrence p(H&D), Fisherian p(D|H), likelihood subtraction, base rate only.
numbers: Study 2: 15 Konstanz students. Bayesian algorithms 60 with relative frequencies vs 66 with probabilities (no difference). In probability format 6.4% Bayesian in the standard menu rising about 3x in the short menu. In Study 1 Bayesian algorithms were 34.9% of all coded solutions overall (620 of 1,774); 84% of solutions were identifiable.
limits: Small N in Study 2. Study 2 ran before Study 1.
agent_relevance: The fix is the information structure (counts of joint events), not a different-looking percent. Implement as: build the 2x2 table of counts in code.

source: Chapman & Liu (2009) Numeracy, frequency, and Bayesian reasoning (Judgment and Decision Making 4)
finding: Replicates the frequency-format advantage but shows it is mostly in high-numeracy people. Correct answers stay rare overall. Common errors: report the hit rate (90%), the base rate (1%), or the correct numerator over the wrong denominator (55 out of 10,000).
numbers: Questionnaire, 346 college students in the table (abstract says 342). Correct answers, high numerates (n = 190): probability 1% (medical) and 7% (car); frequency 27% and 31%. Low numerates (n = 156): probability 0% and 1%; frequency 7% and 10%. Format x numeracy interaction chi2(1) = 13.29, p = .0003. Medical task: correct 47.62% (90 of 189).
limits: Two scenarios, college students, online. Probability column values read from a garbled table.
agent_relevance: The format fix has a floor: the model still has to do the counting. Run the final division in code, do not trust the model to do the division.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1983) Extensional versus intuitive reasoning: the conjunction fallacy in probability judgment (Psych Review 90)
finding: People rank 'Linda is a bank teller and active in the feminist movement' as more probable than 'Linda is a bank teller'. Representativeness drives the ranking. Fallacy found in direct and indirect tests, in naive and expert samples.
numbers: Rank tests (violation rates, direct test): naive Bill 92%, Linda 89%; informed Bill 86%, Linda 90%; sophisticated (doctoral students in decision science) Bill 83%, Linda 85%. Resemblance ranking agreed with the predicted order in 87% (Bill) and 85% (Linda). Choice between T and T&F: 85% chose T&F (N = 142). 9-point scale (N = 119): mean 3.5 for T vs 5.6 for T&F, 82% rated T&F higher.
quote: Surprised by the finding, we searched for alternative interpretations of the subjects' responses.
limits: Rating and ranking tasks. 'Probable' was later argued to be ambiguous in ordinary language (not tested here).
agent_relevance: A model trained on human text inherits the same pull. In code, enforce P(A and B) <= min(P(A), P(B)) on every probability the agent produces.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1983) Extensional versus intuitive reasoning
finding: Ways that reduce but do not remove the fallacy: betting, clarifying the inclusion ('whether or not'), and especially asking in frequencies. Wording 'bank teller whether or not she is active' (T*) still got lower ratings than T&F.
numbers: Bet on T or T&F: 56% fallacy (n = 60). T* vs T&F: mean 3.8 vs 5.1; 57% (n = 75) rated T&F higher, 16% lower. Between subjects: T 3.3, T* 3.9, T&F 4.5. Argument choice: 65% (n = 58) picked the invalid resemblance argument.
limits: Between-subjects cells differ in N; students at UBC and Stanford.
agent_relevance: A direct comparison of nested events does not cure the error in people; the agent needs a check in code, not a reminder in the prompt (links to guardrail G5).

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1983) Extensional versus intuitive reasoning
finding: Frequency wording shrinks the conjunction error. Heart-attack survey: asking for percentages of men gave many violations; asking 'how many of 100 participants' and estimating the constituent class first reduced them.
numbers: Percent version: 65% of respondents (N = 147) gave a strictly higher estimate to the conjunction. Frequency version: 25% (N = 117). Asking for both constituents first: 11% (N = 360). Conditional version mean 59% vs conjunction mean 45%.
limits: Medical scenario only; students.
agent_relevance: Same message as a11: represent the question as counts of cases and ask for the parent class before the subclass.

source: Wu & Gentner (1998) Structure in category-based induction (Cognitive Science Society)
finding: When people choose between an inference from a shared attribute and one from a shared causal antecedent, they prefer the causal one. This favours structural alignment over pure feature overlap (Sloman 1993) or taxonomy-based coverage (Osherson 1990).
numbers: Exp 1: 16 Northwestern undergraduates, 16 items; 13 of 16 predominantly causal (13 or more of 16 trials), none predominantly attribute, p<.05. Exp 2: 16 undergraduates, 12 items; 14 of 16 predominantly causal (11 or more of 12), 1 attribute, 1 at chance.
limits: Tiny samples. Authors note a salience confound (causal info was one long sentence) and stimulus effects (causal consequents may be more enduring).
agent_relevance: Explanations that link cause to effect carry more weight in human induction than lists of shared features. The agent should prefer hypotheses that say why, and test them.

source: Han, Ransom, Perfors & Kemp (2023) Inductive reasoning in humans and large language models
finding: GPT-4 mostly matches human property-induction phenomena (similarity, specificity, typicality, monotonicity). It fails at premise non-monotonicity. GPT-3.5 does poorly and often reacts to argument order.
numbers: Exp 1: 110 people after excluding 10, 792 possible argument pairs, 3 domains (mammals, birds, vehicles) x 24 categories, 11 phenomena. GPT-4 for the Specific non-monotonicity arguments chooses the opposite of people and gives 'more examples make the conclusion stronger' as its reason. Exp 2: replication of 36 Osherson arguments with 40 people, Spearman .65 (p<.001) with the 1990 rankings.
quote: the only notable exception is its failure to capture the phenomenon of premise non-monotonicity
limits: Old models (gpt-4-0314, text-davinci-003). Diversity, asymmetry and inclusion fallacy were not robust even in humans.
agent_relevance: Even strong LLMs treat extra evidence as always raising confidence. Irrelevant or atypical premises can lower support. The agent needs a check that adds evidence only if it is relevant.

source: Han, Ransom, Perfors & Kemp (2023) Inductive reasoning in humans and large language models
finding: Experiment 2 compares models to human ratings. A Human-SCM benchmark (SCM on human similarity ratings) is best overall. GPT-4 nearly matches it on Specific arguments but is uncorrelated with humans on single-premise General mammals arguments. GPT-3.5 is better than GPT-4 on General arguments. Feeding GPT-4 similarities into SCM improves General arguments.
numbers: Best prompt included two practice trials. 600 two-premise and 568 one-premise arguments, GPT-4 queried once at temperature 0, 400-token cap. GPT-4 vs human similarity ratings correlation above .6 in all three domains. Split-half reliability of multi-premise General ratings was low, so those were not interpreted.
limits: Spearman correlations; one run per argument; prompt choices explored only partly.
agent_relevance: A hybrid works: let the model supply similarity numbers and let code apply SCM or a Bayesian rule. Prompt wording and practice examples change results, so test them.

source: Wang, Zelikman, Poesia, Pu, Haber & Goodman (2024) Hypothesis Search: inductive reasoning with language models (ICLR)
finding: Framing induction as posterior prediction, the pipeline has the LLM propose natural-language hypotheses, turn each into Python, and test it on the examples. Hypotheses at two levels of abstraction beat direct output prediction.
numbers: ARC, random 100 tasks, GPT-4, top-1: direct 17%, program only 23%, summarised hypotheses 30%, human-selected hypotheses 33%, human-written hypotheses 45%. Method for summarised: 64 hypotheses summarised to 8, 8 programs each, 3 execution-feedback rounds. Icecuber (non-LLM DSL search) 43%. Only 49 of 100 tasks had a correct hypothesis among the candidates.
quote: our automated pipeline using LLM summaries achieves 30% accuracy, outperforming the direct prompting baseline (accuracy of 17%)
limits: GPT-4 (2023), single subset of 100 tasks, top-1 not the official top-3 scoring. Costs up to $1.5 to test one candidate hypothesis.
agent_relevance: This is the schema's S2 to S4 loop in miniature. Hypothesis then code then test on examples. The bottleneck is generating one correct hypothesis, not implementing it.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Hypothesis Search
finding: Ablations: language alone without programs does not help; execution feedback helps and then plateaus. A program that passes all training cases almost always passes the test case.
numbers: Chain-of-thought hypotheses without code: 19%. Feedback rounds 0/1/2/3: summarised 24/28/28/30, human-selected 26/31/33/33, human-written 38/44/45/45. Of 30 tasks solved by summarised hypotheses, 28 had a correct hypothesis before summarising. One exception to 'train pass implies test pass' found in 100 tasks.
limits: G3 in our schema warns that fitting examples is not proof; here the authors say it nearly was, on this benchmark with a held-out test input.
agent_relevance: Use verification by running code, with held-out cases, to select among hypotheses. Cap the feedback rounds at about two.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Hypothesis Search
finding: On easier inductive benchmarks the gain from hypotheses plus code is larger and less costly.
numbers: 1D-ARC (108 tasks): direct 39.6%, program only 61.1%, full 73.1% (16 hypotheses x 4 programs). List Functions (100 tasks): direct 31%, program only 59%, full 69% (64 hypotheses x 1 program). SyGuS (89 tasks): GPT-4 programs correct on 94.3% with 8 programs; CrossBeam baseline 74.8%.
limits: Different tasks have different sampling budgets. Direct 1D-ARC number is from Xu et al.
agent_relevance: Where the model already has a foothold, hypothesis search helps most (matches guardrail G12). Where the correct hypothesis never appears, extra sampling does not fix it.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Hypothesis Search
finding: Failure cases: hypotheses that are right but hard to code, and language ambiguity that mismatches the program generator ('color pattern' read as the first three columns). The model's own wording of the hypothesis sometimes works better than the human wording.
numbers: Human-written hypotheses 45% vs model-written better match in at least one task (363442ee). A bigger search with Parsel raised human-written to 47.5% but did not help model-written hypotheses.
limits: Anecdotal examples from a few tasks.
agent_relevance: Pair the hypothesis writer and the code writer (same model or same style). Handing a human-style description to a code stage can lose accuracy.

source: Gigerenzer & Hoffrage (1995) How to improve Bayesian reasoning without instruction
finding: Classic base-rate neglect problem and the structure of the fix. Mammography: 1% prevalence, 80% sensitivity, 9.6% false positive rate; the Bayesian answer is 7.8%. Eddy (1982) reported physicians estimating 70% to 80%. In natural frequencies: 10 of 1,000 have cancer; 8 of those test positive; 95 of the other 990 test positive; so 8 out of 103.
quote: The probability of breast cancer is 1% for a woman at age forty who participates in routine screening.
limits: Textbook problem from a 1995 review; physician estimates cited from Eddy (1982), not re-measured here.
agent_relevance: Gives a ready unit test for the probability tool: this problem must come out at 7.8% not 80%.

source: Osherson, Smith, Wilkie, Lopez & Shafir (1990) Category-based induction (Psych Review 97)
finding: Search-page abstract only: argument strength rises with the similarity of the premise categories to the conclusion category and with their similarity to the lowest-level category containing both. The similarity-coverage model accounts for 13 qualitative phenomena.
numbers: 13 qualitative phenomena; 604 Scopus citations on the repository page.
limits: Original paper not opened. All detail on the model comes from later papers (a01, a05, a07, a18).
agent_relevance: Founding paper of the subfield. Next step: obtain full text for exact premise-diversity and typicality numbers.

source: Heit (1998) A Bayesian analysis of some forms of inductive reasoning (in Oaksford & Chater, Rational models of cognition)
finding: Described by Kemp & Tenenbaum: Heit's model has a prior and an inference engine. Evidence is combined with a prior over properties; the prior is suggested to come from properties retrieved from memory, with no formal way to generate it.
numbers: None read from the source.
limits: Not opened; no full text found. Description is second-hand from a01.
agent_relevance: A weak precedent for drawing the prior from the model's own memory. Our schema should check such priors against data instead of trusting them.

source: Chapman & Liu (2009) Numeracy, frequency, and Bayesian reasoning
finding: Bounds the Gigerenzer claim that frequencies work for everyone: the authors say 'the facilitative effect ... does not appear to be universal' and that natural frequencies help only some reasoners.
numbers: Logistic regression: numeracy chi2(1) = 17.78, p = .0001; format main effect chi2(1) = 3.61, p = .06.
quote: Natural frequencies benefit only some types of reasoners.
limits: Online sample; numeracy measure is self-report-like scale items.
agent_relevance: For the agent: format change is necessary but not sufficient. The arithmetic must be handed to code.

source: Han et al. (2023) Inductive reasoning in humans and large language models
finding: Design of a benchmark: 11 phenomena (similarity, specificity, typicality, monotonicity, diversity, non-monotonicity, asymmetry, inclusion fallacy and others), each with General and Specific forms and paired arguments of the form {premises} -> conclusion.
numbers: 24 categories per domain; examples: Diversity {pig, wolf, fox}->gorilla vs {pig, wolf}->gorilla style pairs; Non-monotonicity {crow, peacock}->bird vs {crow, peacock, rabbit}->bird. Code and data are public.
limits: Pairs were chosen to be at least 0.75 SD apart on norms, so effects are strong by design.
agent_relevance: A ready test set for checking whether our induction step handles diversity and non-monotonicity. Cheap to run.

source: Wu & Gentner (1998) Structure in category-based induction
finding: Describes the rival formal accounts: SCM uses hierarchical relations between categories; Sloman's feature-coverage model has no hierarchy and relates strength to feature overlap and inversely to the familiarity and complexity of the conclusion category.
numbers: None; framing section.
limits: Conference paper, short.
agent_relevance: Three families of induction scores exist (taxonomic coverage, feature overlap, structural alignment). Any one can be written in code. Which one applies depends on the property type.

source: Tenenbaum, Kemp & Shafto (2007) Theory-based Bayesian models of inductive reasoning
finding: Argues the Bayesian engine is a computational-level account, not a claim about processes. It models only the content of intuitive theories as priors. Two ingredients are both needed: domain-specific prior knowledge and a general Bayesian inference engine.
numbers: None.
quote: minimalist accounts, intended to capture only
limits: Authors defend their own approach; they state they are agnostic about mental processes.
agent_relevance: Fits the schema split: the model supplies the prior knowledge (structure, similarity); the program does the inference.
